sources.news_title: Cornell president acknowledges missteps as university faces leadership crisis
Cornell president admits he never followed up on gang rape allegation ahead of no-confidence debate - Boston News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff knew in 2024 that a student had reported being gang raped at a fraternity house, but never followed up to learn what had happened to her or whether any of the accused students had been punished.
In an interview with The New York Times published Tuesday, a day before Cornell’s Faculty Senate began debating a no-confidence resolution in his administration, Kotlikoff acknowledged that he did not know until recently that the woman had dropped out of Cornell or that students had been expelled or suspended over the incident.
Kotlikoff publicly addressed what he called “deeply disturbing” allegations involving drug use and sexual violence at the Chi Phi fraternity house in a November 2024 message to the Cornell community, saying criminal and university investigations were underway.
He subsequently convened a presidential task force to examine how Cornell handles sexual assault, but said this week that he never followed up to learn the outcomes of the criminal or Title IX investigations into the woman’s allegations.
Faculty describe ‘contentious’ meeting
The faculty senate meeting stretched past the two hours anticipated. Kotlikoff left the meeting after addressing faculty members and answering questions, and did not stay for the debate over the no-confidence resolution, according to Anne Marie Brady, a co-sponsor who attended.
Faculty described a contentious meeting that exposed a division on campus on what should happen next.
“The institution is split in significant ways,” said Grant Farred, professor of Africana Studies and English, describing those in the humanities as feeling they had enough information to proceed while those in the sciences wanted more data.
Iris Packman, a member of the faculty senate and senior research and policy development associate at Cornell’s ILR School Climate Jobs Institute, said the meeting had a “contentious tone” and that Kotlikoff got “defensive” and tried to “control the narrative.”
“The resolution is about the need for systematic change because there is a systematic problem,” Packman said. The underlying case happened in 2024 but “the administration has yet to take responsibility for anything,” she said.
Debate was expected to continue Oct. 28, followed by electronic voting by the Faculty Senate, which has approximately 130 voting members. A simple majority is required for passage.
Case has drawn national attention, roiled campus
The case has drawn national attention since the woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit alleging that seven Chi Phi fraternity members sexually assaulted or exploited her in October 2024 and that Cornell mishandled her complaints.
On Tuesday, Kotlikoff announced a ban on fraternity parties through the end of the academic year and plans to give state police a role in investigating sexual assault reports.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue charges after reviewing a summary prepared by Cornell University Police, but later said it omitted key details. He reopened the investigation after the lawsuit was filed. Gov. Kathy Hochul subsequently removed him from the case, appointed Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor and ordered an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the allegations.
The Cornell Faculty Senate’s proposed resolution, declaring no confidence in the administration’s ability to handle reports of sexual assault on campus, reflects growing concerns among some faculty members that people who report sexual misconduct face institutional barriers and fear retaliation. Some have called for Kotlikoff’s resignation, while others have urged patience as independent investigations proceed.
The resolution is nonbinding and would not force Kotlikoff or other university leaders from office, but cosponsors said they hoped it would prompt Cornell’s trustees and senior administrators to act.
Faculty members question whether Cornell can investigate itself
Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct.
“There doesn’t seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department,” Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside law enforcement agencies.
Brady welcomed Kotlikoff’s announcement that state police would take on a role in sexual assault investigations, saying it showed the administration was listening to faculty concerns. But she questioned the timing, a day before the Senate was scheduled to begin debating the no-confidence resolution.
“I’m happy that they are listening — we need a dialogue,” she said. “We need to debate and discuss this. But I also feel it’s a bit disingenuous that it comes out just before the resolution.”
Professor who reported harassment says it nearly cost her career
For Ariana Kim, an associate music professor at Cornell and co-sponsor of the resolution, Kotlikoff’s acknowledgment that he had not followed up on the woman’s case was deeply troubling.
“I mean, that’s appalling in and of itself, right?” Kim said. “That you don’t know about a student who faced an alleged horrific crime, that you don’t think to check in.”
Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe’s story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken.
“I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation,” she said.
Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues she said had harassed her. Her efforts to avoid them later became a point of criticism during her tenure review. In one instance, a senior professor cited her unwillingness to accept his advice and her avoidance of him in explaining his vote against granting her tenure.
Kim spent more than a year appealing the initial denial of tenure, a process during which she said she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. The original decision was ultimately overturned, and she secured tenure.
Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career.
“I’m speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion,” she said.
Kotlikoff has faced other challenges during his tenure
The controversy over Cornell’s handling of sexual assault allegations is the latest challenge for Kotlikoff, who became the university’s interim president in July 2024, months before Jane Doe’s alleged assault, and took the job permanently last year.
Dining and custodial workers went on strike shortly after he took office, and some faculty and students criticized his decision last year to pay $60 million to settle Trump administration civil rights investigations.
Earlier this year, he also faced accusations that he tried to back his car into demonstrators following a campus debate over Israel and Palestinian rights. Kotlikoff denied the allegations, saying he was the victim of harassment.

sources.news_title: Tragic Cornell Case Demonstrates Why Biblical Values Are Not Outdated
sources.text:
Tragic Cornell Case Demonstrates Why Biblical Values Are Not Outdated
In the wake of the ongoing sexual assault case at Cornell University, school president Michael I. Kotlikoff has banned parties and social events at campus fraternity houses – the latest response to a gang-rape allegation dating to 2024.
“I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society,” wrote Kotlikoff.
The Ithaca-based school’s leader then dropped the hammer, declaring:
“Any fraternity holding an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension.”
It was back in September that “Jane Doe” filed a 101-page civil complaint alleging that she and her sorority sisters went out drinking one night back in October 2024. She reported that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by numerous men inside afraternity house on the Cornell campus.
The complaint acknowledges that the victim waited three weeks to report the incident to campus police, who then proceeded to investigate the alleged crime. “Jane Doe” explained that given the trauma and shock of the assault, it took some time for her to process what had happened.
Following the investigation, university officials identified and pursued the accusedattackers. Kyle Kimball, who serves as Cornell’s spokesperson, told the Washington Post, “Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false.”
He added:
“A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”
Those “consequences” included closing down one of the fraternities and suspending seven students from the school. At the time, university police also turned over the complaint to the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office. The DA declined to prosecute citing, “insufficient evidence.”
Late last month, the district attorney’s office, under fire for not pursuing the case back in 2024, agreed to reopen the investigation given new evidence. In defending their initial decision, the DA wrote:
Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later. Furthermore, I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations.
Roughly one-third of Cornell’s 16,000 undergraduate students are part of a fraternity or sorority.
Fraternities in America date back to the Revolutionary War and, not surprisingly, looked nothing then like they do today. The College of William & Mary in Virginia holds the distinction of being the first school to host one on campus. Known as “Phi Beta Kappa” or “Philosophia Biou Kybernētēs,” which means “Love of wisdom is the guide of life,” it was considered a secret society.
The focus of the group wasn’t alcohol-laden parties but rather intellectual conversation and debate. There was a strong literary component and influence, too. Given the American colonist’s growing rebellion against Great Britain, students also discussed the unfolding war and the nation’s future as an independent country.
Popularity of these private college groups grew quickly over the years. By the 1800s, Greek letter societies became less secret and more social, best known as safe places to develop friendships and network with fellow students and alumni. Members dined together and may have socialized over drinks at times, but it wasn’t the main focal point or purpose of the group.
Studies suggest this began to change steadily and then significantly in the 20th century with official concerns related to excessive alcohol consumption emerging as early as the 1940s. In modern history, the fraternity-drinking scene became culturally entrenched beginning in 1978 with the release of the raucous and crass film “Animal House.”
Of course, while popular culture often associates fraternities and sororities with alcohol-infused parties, there are many college groups bucking that stereotype. For example, Union University in Jackson, Tenn, states their goal is “to produce Christian men and women who view life through the lens of Scripture and act accordingly to God-given wisdom and integrity.” They suggest, “Greek life at Union seeks to support the university in reaching this goal by developing men and women of integrity.”
Abilene Christian University notes that it “supports the efforts of Greek Life to stimulate a closer bond of friendship among students and enhance each student’s loyalty to ACU.”
We’ve recently noted the attention some universities and colleges receive for being a “party school” – a distinction that should stand as a warning to parents and students alike. Over the years, popular culture has often mocked the Christian virtues of abstinence and temperance. Whether in movies, television, or music, self-restraint is depicted as being prudish and somehow detached from reality.
In reality, the heartbreaking Cornell University sexual assault case tragedy demonstrates why biblical virtues are not outdated relics but essential guides for protecting the dignity and well-being of women and men in every season of life.

Paul J. Batura is a writer and vice president of communications for Focus on the Family. He’s authored numerous books including “Chosen for Greatness: How Adoption Changes the World,” “Good Day! The Paul Harvey Story” and “Mentored by the King: Arnold Palmer's Success Lessons for Golf, Business, and Life.” Paul can be reached via email: Paul.Batura@fotf.org or Twitter @PaulBatura

Kim, a Grammy-nominated violinist, said she was motivated to take action after being struck by Jane Doe's story, as well as her own personal experiences on campus since she started at Cornell a decade ago as a young academic in her 20s. She said when she experienced bullying and sexual harassment by senior colleagues, Cornell failed to properly document her complaints and that she was never clearly informed what disciplinary action, if any, had been taken.
“I was asked what I had done to provoke the situation,” she said.
Kim said she continued to be expected to work alongside colleagues involved in the dispute. She believes reporting the misconduct later affected her tenure review.
She spent 18 months appealing an adverse tenure decision, a process during which she lost 20 pounds (9 kilograms) and struggled to eat or sleep. A university appeals board ultimately overturned the original decision, and she secured tenure.
Now seeking promotion to full professor, Kim said she recognizes that publicly criticizing university leaders could again jeopardize her career.
“I’m speaking out publicly against this administration that may very well deny my promotion,” she said.
Kim said she has considered leaving Cornell many times over the years but is determined to stay and make the university safer for those who come after her.
“If by me fighting, it helps move the needle a little bit so that my female students aren’t going through this in 10 years or my female colleagues aren’t going through this in five years, then maybe it’s worth it.”

Anne Marie Brady, a senior extension associate at Cornell’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations and another co-sponsor of the resolution, questioned whether Cornell University Police can independently investigate serious allegations of sexual misconduct.
“There doesn’t seem to be independence between the administration and the Cornell Police Department,” Brady said. She pointed to its handling of campus protests as one reason for her concerns and said serious criminal allegations should be investigated by outside law enforcement agencies.

“I’m happy that they are listening — we need a dialogue,” she said. “We need to debate and discuss this. But I also feel it’s a bit disingenuous that it comes out just before the resolution.”

sources.news_title: Cornell president faces scrutiny in contentious meeting with faculty during no-confidence debate
Cornell Faculty Senate debates no-confidence vote in administration
sources.text:
Cornell University’s Faculty Senate began debating a vote of no confidence in the university’s administration on Wednesday in response to the initial handling of 2024 gang rape allegations that have since put the university in the national spotlight.
The measure is largely symbolic and would not automatically terminate any administrators if passed.
Senators who support the measure say they’re frustrated by the current climate around sexual assault on campus, one that they say has been built by years of administrations choosing to sweep dirt under the rug rather than protect survivors.
“It is a signal that they need to do better and that we’re watching. We want to hold them accountable,” said Iris Packman, one of several faculty senators who co-sponsored the resolution.
It’s not just the university’s senate; at a “Justice for Jane Doe” rally on Tuesday, protesters also condemned the administration’s response so far.
“I’m angry at the perpetrators at Cornell’s administration for continuously failing Jane Doe,” said Jesser Romero Silver, a student from Ithaca College who spoke at the rally.
Hours before the rally, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff released a statement saying he is deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024 and announced several changes aimed at strengthening campus safety and better supporting survivors, including reforming and refocusing the Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault and banning all fraternity parties and social events through the end of the school year.
Jane Doe supporters and victim advocates in general, however, say they’d prefer to see a permanent ban for those parties.
“Certainly, banning fraternity parties for the duration of this academic year will have some effect, but it’s not, again, taking accountability for that major cultural problem,” Packman said.
Dr. Kate Bronfenbrenner is a retired faculty member who says she’s spent most of her life on or around Cornell’s campus. She says the newly announced changes aren’t enough to combat the long-standing culture around sexual assault on campus.
“I had friends who were assaulted when I was an undergraduate. I remember when I was a graduate student, there was a flyer for a fraternity party that said, ‘gang rape party,’” Dr. Bronfenbrenner recalled. “That was 1986, around that time, so this is not new.”
The issue is not specific to Cornell; sexual assault has been an issue on many other college campuses over the years, as well.
“I’m sorry that this is still going on,” said Leisa Creo, who traveled from New York City to rally in support of Jane Doe on Tuesday. “It was going on when we were in college too, and we should have done more.”
As Cornell’s Faculty Senate continues to debate a vote of no confidence, protesters and advocates hope the continued international scrutiny and local demonstrations continue to drive what’s now become a movement to protect all survivors.
Cornell’s Faculty Senate will meet again on Oct. 28 to continue discussing the measure. A vote is expected to take place in the following days.

Cornell University’s faculty senate will begin to debate today a resolution of no confidence in the school’s administration. It is the latest escalation in a crisis that began with a civil lawsuit filed last month alleging an extreme sexual assault at a campus fraternity in 2024. Here is what the resolution means, what is happening today, and how the university got here.
What are the allegations?
In September 2026, a former Cornell student identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit alleging that seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity drugged and gang-raped her at a fraternity house on October 19, 2024, when she was 20 years old. The lawsuit alleged that one of the men used Snapchat to invite other fraternity members to join, and included a photograph of that chat. None of the seven men have been criminally charged, and all have denied wrongdoing.
Cornell’s own Title IX investigation resulted in the expulsion of two men and lesser punishments for the others. The local district attorney declined to prosecute in 2024, but has since reopened the case this fall after the lawsuit was filed. New York Attorney General Letitia James has now taken over the criminal investigation as a special prosecutor at the request of Governor Kathy Hochul.
What has Cornell done in response?
On Tuesday, university president Michael Kotlikoff announced a ban on all fraternity parties and related social events for the remainder of the academic year. The university plans to hire independent, trauma-informed criminal investigators to examine sexual assault allegations on campus. The investigators will be independent of Cornell and will prepare investigative summaries for law enforcement. The university also announced it will expand staffing in its civil rights office and implement changes following an independent review led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates.
What is the no-confidence resolution?
The faculty senate is debating a single-sentence resolution: “The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.” The resolution does not call for specific resignations or policy mandates. Rather, it is a formal condemnation.
The measure was co-sponsored by a dozen senate members, and a majority vote is required to pass. There are currently 136 voting members listed on Cornell’s faculty senate website.
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” said Professor Paul Ortiz, the resolution’s lead sponsor, in a statement to ABC News.

President Kotlikoff and Provost Kavita Bala will address the senate and take questions before debate on the resolution begins. Members of Cornell’s Sexual Assault Task Force and the director of sexual harassment and assault response are also scheduled to speak. The final 30 minutes of the 90-minute session will open formal debate.
The university is prohibiting all photography and video recording of the meeting and restricting entry to those with Cornell IDs. ABC News reports that organizers have said a recording will be released later in the week.

A second debate session is scheduled for October 28. Voting will take place online over five days following that meeting.

sources.news_title: Cornell Senate to debate no-confidence resolution in administrators amid rape case
sources.text:
Cornell Senate to debate no-confidence resolution in administrators amid rape case
ITHACA, N.Y. (WSTM) — Cornell University Senators are set to debate a resolution declaring "no confidence" in administrators on Wednesday.
Senators announced their intention to hold a vote on Oct. 6. It follows weeks of protests and national scrutiny of how the university handled an October 2024 case of an alleged rape at the Chi Phi fraternity.
On Wednesday, the Senate held the debate over the resolution at 4:30 p.m. on Wednesday. A second debate will follow on Oct. 28. The vote will be held electronically on an unannounced date following both debates.
A faculty committee spent days reviewing the resolution before it heads to the full Cornell University Senate. The resolution would ask faculty to formally declare that they have lost confidence in the university administration. The Senate has more than 75 voting members and serves as the primary legislative, advisory and review body representing Cornell faculty.
A no-confidence vote expresses serious dissatisfaction with an administration and can increase pressure on university leadership to act. The resolution is being led by Senator Paul Ortiz.
In September, a civil lawsuit by "Jane Joe" accused seven men of pressuring her to consume ketamine and gang-raping her at the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024 and into the early morning hours the next day.
Jane Doe reported the October 2024 incident to Cornell Police in the following days. The university then conducted a months-long investigation into the matter. The university said its investigation led to expulsions and suspensions. The Chi Phi fraternity was also suspended and barred from campus.
No criminal charges were ever filed as a result of Cornell's investigation, prompting Jane Doe to follow up with the civil lawsuit.
On Oct. 13, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff announced that the campus would suspend all parties and social events in Interfraternity Council houses for the remainder of the 2026-2027 academic year. President Kotlikoff also promised better support systems for survivors of sexual assault.
Still, just hours after the president's announcement, students, survivors of sexual assault and Ithaca neighbors gathered in the city's popular Ithaca Commons to rally in support of Jane Doe. The "I Am Jane Doe" rally saw hundreds of people come out to demand accountability from Cornell administrators.
The rally was just the latest in student-led activism demanding change at Cornell. Just one week earlier, hundreds took over the Ho Plaza on campus for the "Justice for Survivors" rally, calling on university leaders to change how sexual assault cases are handled.
Students for a Democratic Cornell organized the rally. They brought with them a list of five demands. They are:
- Expulsion or degree revocation for anyone found responsible for involvement in the alleged rape of the student identified as Jane Doe.
- Changes to Cornell’s Policy 6.4 to require independent hearings and minimum sanctions in sexual assault cases.
- An external investigation of Cornell’s administration and a return to an independent judicial system.
- Mandatory sexual assault prevention training for students and trauma-informed training for Cornell University Police.
- Full compliance with New York’s “Enough is Enough” law.
New York State Attorney General Letitia James is investigating the alleged rape. She said her office will pursue criminal charges if the evidence warrants it. Her investigation is expected to take months.

sources.news_title: Cornell University President Apologizes To Jane Doe
sources.text:
Cornell University President Apologizes To Jane Doe
Cornell President To Jane Doe I'm Personally Sorry For Your Experience
Dr. Michael Kotlikoff -- the president of Cornell University -- is personally apologizing to Jane Doe for her experience at the Ivy League school ... and it sounds like he won't resign.
The New York Times sat down with Kotlikoff for a wide-ranging interview, and he said he was "personally sorry" for everything Doe says she experienced when she was enrolled at Cornell.
While he's deeply sorry, the interview also revealed just how in the dark Kotlikoff says he was about the original investigation into her sexual assault claims ... he says he didn't read hundreds of pages of confidential records put together during the Title IX investigation out of respect for students' privacy.
Kotlikoff says the administration has more information now than it did during the 2024 investigation ... but Scott Schneider -- a Title IX lawyer and adviser -- told the NYT that a university president can look through the entire Title IX investigation when reviewing such material if it serves a "legitimate institutional purpose."
Basically, Kotlikoff could've looked through the case to refine the college's processes regarding sexual assault complaints ... but he decided not to.
Kotlikoff says he wasn't informed when the Tompkins County District Attorney decided not to charge anyone ... and he also wasn't notified when Doe dropped out of school.
Despite all the issues, Kotlikoff says he's not stepping down ... though it may not end up being his call. The faculty senate is expected to hold a vote of no confidence later this month.
Cornell is taking steps to curb on-campus drug and alcohol use ... with Kotlikoff announcing Tuesday that fraternities are prohibited from holding parties through the rest of the academic year.

sources.news_title: Cornell University faculty weigh no-confidence resolution
Cornell University faculty to begin debating no-confidence resolution
sources.text:
Approximately 150 faculty members are said to be in support of the resolution.
Cornell University’s faculty senate on Wednesday will begin deliberating a no-confidence resolution to condemn the school’s response to sexual violence on campus.
One month after allegations of a “gang rape” at a campus fraternity shook the Ivy League school, the resolution, if adopted, could mark the clearest repudiation of Cornell’s leadership since the controversy began.
“We're saying we have no confidence in how the administration has handled this. It is a crisis. It's a long-term systemic problem. Jane Doe's case is significant, but it is not nearly the only case like this,” Iris Packman, a faculty senator, told ABC News.
Cornell University’s president and provost are scheduled to address the faculty senate and take questions before the debate begins, and the formal vote on the resolution is set to take place later this month.
“What we are wanting is real effective leadership, not just reactive responses by the central administration,” said Professor Risa Lieberwitz, another member of the faculty senate.
What does the resolution call for?
Cornell’s faculty senate is debating adopting a one-sentence resolution that reads, “The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” Professor Paul Ortiz, the lead sponsor for the resolution, told ABC News via email.
According to Packman, approximately 150 faculty members have signaled their support for the resolution, and the measure was co-sponsored by a dozen members of the faculty senate. For the resolution to pass, the measure would need support from a majority of the faculty senate.
Cornell’s faculty senate is a “governing body that supports faculty communication toward successful management of objectives for the University,” according to the school. Academic titleholders at Cornell -- including professors, senior lecturers, librarians, archivists and others -- are eligible to be senators, who serve three-year terms.
The resolution itself does not call for specific action -- such as demanding resignations or forcing policy changes -- and instead offers a broad condemnation of the school’s response.
“I think it's important that we did not specifically call for [the] resignations of anybody. We are not saying XYZ administrators need to leave, but these ones are okay. We're saying we don't have confidence in the way that they are handling this, and we don't have confidence that they are going to effectively address it going forward,” said Packman, one of the co-sponsors of the resolution.
What is scheduled to take place on Wednesday?
The bulk of Wednesday’s meeting is centered on remarks and presentations from Cornell’s leadership, according to the meeting agenda.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and Provost Kavita Bala are scheduled to deliver remarks and answer questions before members of the school’s Sexual Assault Task Force address the group. Cornell’s director of sexual harassment and assault response is also set to address the senators before taking questions. The final 30 minutes of the 90-minute meeting is scheduled to begin debate of the resolution.
Cornell’s dean of faculty is also set to address the body to read an “expressive activity statement.” Past faculty senate meetings have not begun with that kind of statement, according to Professor Lieberwitz, and the purpose and content of those remarks are not clear.
Cornell finalized its “expressive activity policy” last year in the aftermath of campus protests. It allows the school to restrict speech if it “disrupts essential operations necessary for the teaching, research, patient care, or residential campus missions of the university.”
“A zealous commitment to freedom of expression does not mean that anyone can say anything they like, whenever and however they like,” the policy says.
Packman argued that the statement may have a “chilling effect on faculty speech” by discouraging some speakers, particularly senators who do not have the protections afforded by tenure.
“If we're having a statement read telling us what we can and can't say and how we can and can't say it before we even engage in that debate, that is a significant overstep and restriction on our speech,” she said.
When is the vote scheduled to take place?
Deliberations over the resolution are set to take place on Wednesday, as well as a meeting on Oct. 28, according to the resolution.
Voting on the resolution is scheduled to take place after the October 28 meeting and last for five days. The voting will take place online, according to organizers.
Will the meeting be recorded?
Cornell University is prohibiting photography or video recording of Wednesday's meeting. Only individuals with Cornell ID will be allowed to enter the auditorium where the meeting will take place.
According to organizers, a recording of the meeting will be released by Cornell later this week.
What measures did Cornell announce on Tuesday?
Wednesday’s meeting comes on the heels of an announcement by President Kotlikoff about measures to “strengthen campus safety, better support survivors, and begin addressing the social context of sexual violence at Cornell.”
Cornell suspended all social events and parties held by fraternities while the school conducts a “review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.”
The school also vowed to add more staff to its Office of Civil Rights -- which conducts Title IX investigations -- as well as report allegations of sexual assault to the New York State Police during the school’s review of its policies.
“We are working with the New York State Police to allow their experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on campus. These individuals will interview survivors who elect to pursue criminal charges and will prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency,” the statement said.
Kotlikoff also vowed to implement changes proposed by Cornell’s Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault, as well as “re-form and re-focus” that entity to examine “opportunities for safe and healthy social engagement and further ways to reduce risks.”

sources.news_title: Cornell's Faculty Senate considers no-confidence vote for school's president
sources.text:
Cornell's Faculty Senate considers no-confidence vote for school's president
Cornell says it's making big changes on campus following the allegations of a gang rape, but it remains under fire. The Faculty Senate is now discussing a no-confidence vote of the president.
MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:
Cornell is banning fraternity parties through the end of the year. That's one of several changes the university is making to improve campus safety in response to an allegation that a young woman was raped - gang-raped - at a frat house in 2024. The faculty senate is also scheduled to meet later today. On the agenda? Beginning the process of voting no confidence in university leadership. NPR's Elissa Nadworny is in Ithaca, New York, and she's here to tell us more about this. Good morning.
ELISSA NADWORNY, BYLINE: Good morning.
MARTIN: OK - a ban on frat parties. But what else did the Cornell administration promise to do?
NADWORNY: So Cornell agreed to hire staff to help students as they navigate reporting sexual misconduct. They also said they would hire criminal investigators - so those are independent of Cornell - that would look into allegations of sexual assault on campus. They're also going to add things like more bystander training.
In a letter announcing these changes, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff wrote that they were the first step towards systematic change. He pledged to address what he called deeply disturbing prevalence of alcohol and drug abuse on campus.
MARTIN: You know, like, recognizing that there's - there are different constituencies on every campus - like, there's faculty. There's staff. There's students - do people on campus think that's enough?
NADWORNY: Well, I talked with a student who said the ban on frat parties felt more like good PR, a headline, than actual culture change. And professors I've talked with say that their trust is still broken, and the way that they're going to communicate that is by asking the faculty to vote no confidence. Today's meeting is going to begin that process. Anne Marie Brady, for example, is a member of the faculty senate who co-signed the motion.
ANNE MARIE BRADY: There's a great sense of anger and, I think, also sadness. We have lost confidence in the administration to effectively address sexual assault and sexual harassment on campus.
NADWORNY: Over the weekend, more than 200 faculty and staff signed a letter to students that said, this administration does not speak for us. They say the university has failed to keep students safe and more change is needed.
MARTIN: Should the president be worried about his job?
NADWORNY: So the faculty doesn't have the power to oust a president. Only the board of trustees can do that. They are also meeting later this week on campus here in Ithaca. Michel, I've been asking this question to professors and students - like, should Kotlikoff step down or be let go? And removing the president was actually not one of the student groups' demands. This is sophomore John Hartnett.
JOHN HARTNETT: We don't want Kotlikoff to go down for the mishandling of Jane Doe's case and then someone to come in and mishandle another case the exact same way. We're focused on the institution changing in a way that that sort of misconduct is structurally much less possible than it is now.
NADWORNY: He said that the changes announced yesterday were kind of a half measure. You know, that said, I was at a protest yesterday where crowds were chanting, Kotlikoff has got to go.
I guess all this to say, Michel, President Kotlikoff and his administration are under a lot of pressure. They've hired an outside investigator to look into what happened back in 2024. That's Sally Yates, who helped lead the U.S. Department of Justice during the Obama administration. And as you may recall, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has already appointed the state attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor to look into the case. I think the policy changes announced yesterday, including the ban on frat parties, really underscore just how much pressure the administration is under.
MARTIN: That is NPR's Elissa Nadworny in Ithaca, New York. Elissa, thanks so much.
NADWORNY: You bet.

One month after allegations of a “gang rape” at a campus fraternity shook the Ivy League school, the resolution, if adopted, could mark the clearest repudiation of Cornell’s leadership since the controversy began.
“We're saying we have no confidence in how the administration has handled this. It is a crisis. It's a long-term systemic problem. Jane Doe's case is significant, but it is not nearly the only case like this,” Iris Packman, a faculty senator, told ABC News.
Cornell University’s president and provost are scheduled to address the faculty senate and take questions before the debate begins, and the formal vote on the resolution is set to take place later this month.
“What we are wanting is real effective leadership, not just reactive responses by the central administration,” said Professor Risa Lieberwitz, another member of the faculty senate.
What does the resolution call for?
Cornell’s faculty senate is debating adopting a one-sentence resolution that reads, “The Faculty Senate has no confidence in the ability of the central administration to effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”
“The key point to understand is that scores of students, staff, faculty and alumni have approached the sponsors of the resolution to emphasize to us that the Jane Doe case is but the tip of the iceberg,” Professor Paul Ortiz, the lead sponsor for the resolution, told ABC News via email.
According to Packman, approximately 150 faculty members have signaled their support for the resolution, and the measure was co-sponsored by a dozen members of the faculty senate. For the resolution to pass, the measure would need support from a majority of the faculty senate.
Cornell’s faculty senate is a “governing body that supports faculty communication toward successful management of objectives for the University,” according to the school. Academic titleholders at Cornell -- including professors, senior lecturers, librarians, archivists and others -- are eligible to be senators, who serve three-year terms.
The resolution itself does not call for specific action -- such as demanding resignations or forcing policy changes -- and instead offers a broad condemnation of the school’s response.
“I think it's important that we did not specifically call for [the] resignations of anybody. We are not saying XYZ administrators need to leave, but these ones are okay. We're saying we don't have confidence in the way that they are handling this, and we don't have confidence that they are going to effectively address it going forward,” said Packman, one of the co-sponsors of the resolution.
What is scheduled to take place on Wednesday?
The bulk of Wednesday’s meeting is centered on remarks and presentations from Cornell’s leadership, according to the meeting agenda.
Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff and Provost Kavita Bala are scheduled to deliver remarks and answer questions before members of the school’s Sexual Assault Task Force address the group. Cornell’s director of sexual harassment and assault response is also set to address the senators before taking questions. The final 30 minutes of the 90-minute meeting is scheduled to begin debate of the resolution.
Cornell’s dean of faculty is also set to address the body to read an “expressive activity statement.” Past faculty senate meetings have not begun with that kind of statement, according to Professor Lieberwitz, and the purpose and content of those remarks are not clear.
Cornell finalized its “expressive activity policy” last year in the aftermath of campus protests. It allows the school to restrict speech if it “disrupts essential operations necessary for the teaching, research, patient care, or residential campus missions of the university.”
“A zealous commitment to freedom of expression does not mean that anyone can say anything they like, whenever and however they like,” the policy says.
Packman argued that the statement may have a “chilling effect on faculty speech” by discouraging some speakers, particularly senators who do not have the protections afforded by tenure.
“If we're having a statement read telling us what we can and can't say and how we can and can't say it before we even engage in that debate, that is a significant overstep and restriction on our speech,” she said.
When is the vote scheduled to take place?
Deliberations over the resolution are set to take place on Wednesday, as well as a meeting on Oct. 28, according to the resolution.
Voting on the resolution is scheduled to take place after the October 28 meeting and last for five days. The voting will take place online, according to organizers.
Will the meeting be recorded?
Cornell University is prohibiting photography or video recording of Wednesday's meeting. Only individuals with Cornell ID will be allowed to enter the auditorium where the meeting will take place.
According to organizers, a recording of the meeting will be released by Cornell later this week.
What measures did Cornell announce on Tuesday?
Wednesday’s meeting comes on the heels of an announcement by President Kotlikoff about measures to “strengthen campus safety, better support survivors, and begin addressing the social context of sexual violence at Cornell.”
Cornell suspended all social events and parties held by fraternities while the school conducts a “review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.”
The school also vowed to add more staff to its Office of Civil Rights -- which conducts Title IX investigations -- as well as report allegations of sexual assault to the New York State Police during the school’s review of its policies.
“We are working with the New York State Police to allow their experienced, trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell University, to investigate allegations of sexual assault on campus. These individuals will interview survivors who elect to pursue criminal charges and will prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency,” the statement said.
Kotlikoff also vowed to implement changes proposed by Cornell’s Presidential Task Force on Sexual Assault, as well as “re-form and re-focus” that entity to examine “opportunities for safe and healthy social engagement and further ways to reduce risks.”
